finding.claim: Unauthenticated Marshal deserialization of attacker-supplied bytes in POST /restore gives remote code execution.
finding.source: HTTP POST parameter params[:state] (app.rb:6), attacker-controlled, reachable by any client that can reach the app.
finding.sink: Marshal.load(Base64.decode64(...)) at app.rb:6, which runs marshal_load/_load/init_with callbacks on any class named in the byte stream.

trace.note: post "/restore" route accepts any unauthenticated POST.
params[:state] is Base64-decoded and passed directly to Marshal.load.
state.inspect returns the reconstructed object's representation to the caller, giving the attacker an output channel.

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization in app.rb. No HMAC or signature on the state blob. No class allowlist (Marshal.load has none). No size limit or content-type check. Rack::Protection defaults do not cover request-body deserialization. Nothing in this file restricts the route. Exploitability depends on Ruby/RubyGems version and loaded gems; not runtime-verified.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5 is an unauthenticated post "/restore" route with no before filter, no auth helper, and no signature or HMAC check on the blob. app.rb:6 calls Marshal.load directly on Base64.decode64(params[:state]) with no class allowlist, size limit, or content-type check. app.rb:7 returns state.inspect to the caller, which gives an output channel. Nothing in app.rb or the Sinatra defaults prevents the call.
verdict.reason: The POST /restore route at app.rb:5 is anonymous, and app.rb:6 passes attacker-controlled params[:state] straight into Marshal.load with no guard, so unsafe deserialization is reachable. The RCE part is not proven here: it depends on gadget classes in the loaded gems, which the candidate itself notes was not runtime-verified, so the confirmed defect is unsafe deserialization with RCE as the likely impact.

finding.claim: POST /import reflects attacker-controlled JSON object keys into an HTML-typed response without escaping, giving reflected XSS.
finding.source: Request body (app.rb:11), attacker-controlled JSON. Object key names are attacker-chosen strings.
finding.sink: Response body at app.rb:12 (data.keys.join(",")), returned under Sinatra's default text/html content type.

trace.note: JSON.parse(request.body.read) returns a Hash with attacker-chosen string keys. JSON.parse does not instantiate objects, so this is not a deserialization issue.
data.keys.join(",") returns raw key strings as the body with no escaping and no explicit Content-Type.

finding.guards_checked: No explicit Content-Type (Sinatra defaults to text/html;charset=utf-8). No HTML escaping (escape_html not used). Rack::Protection XSSHeader sets only the legacy X-XSS-Protection header and does not sanitize the body. JsonCsrf does not apply to text/html. Cross-site delivery is possible via a text/plain HTML form whose name/value split yields valid JSON, so the victim browser can navigate to the reflected response in the app origin without a CSRF token. Not runtime-verified.

verdict.guard_found: None in app.rb: no escape_html, no explicit Content-Type, no auth on the route (app.rb:10-13). The directory has no Gemfile or config.ru, so Sinatra's default Rack::Protection settings cannot be read. Sinatra's default HttpOrigin check (unverified here) would reject cross-site POSTs carrying a foreign Origin header, which is the only route to a victim browser on this POST-only endpoint.
verdict.reason: The trace matches app.rb:10-12 and the body is reflected under text/html, but the cross-site delivery path depends on Sinatra's default Rack::Protection (HttpOrigin) being active, which is not in the available code (app.rb:12 is the only sink line), so this cannot be decided from the files here.
